summary: A conversational, podcast-style interview capturing NarrativeGrid's experience using Redwood Inference to scale personalized content generation for e-commerce recommendations. Focus on outcomes (latency, cost savings, editorial workflow), migration story from a self-hosted prototype to Redwood Hosted + Dedicated, and early KPI wins. Customer agreed to be a featured case study and to record a short testimonial clip.
transcript:
HEADER: 2026-04-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42m | Recording: Zoom | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood Marketing), Ava (NarrativeGrid Head of Growth), Diego (CPO), Priya (ML Eng), Tom (Content)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — excited to have NarrativeGrid on the Redwood podcast. Before we start, audio check, can you hear me okay?
[00:06] Ava (NarrativeGrid): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for having us.
[00:08] Samir (Redwood): Awesome. We'll do this as a casual conversation — if folks want specific technical follow-ups we'll capture those as action items.
[00:15] Tom (NarrativeGrid): Sounds good. I'm, uh, mostly here for the product stories and the editorial bit.
[00:19] Marcus (Redwood): Great. Maybe quick round-robin intros — who you are and what you own at NarrativeGrid?
[00:24] Ava: Sure — I'm Ava, I run growth. I look at how we scale personalization across channels.
[00:28] Diego: Diego here — CPO, responsible for platform and infra choices.
[00:31] Priya: Priya, ML eng — model infra, pipelines.
[00:34] Tom: Tom — content lead, I work with the editorial teams that use the generation outputs.
[00:38] Jordan: Thanks. Okay, jumping in — Ava, tell us the one-sentence problem you were trying to solve with Redwood.
[00:46] Ava: We wanted to make product descriptions and microcopy hyper-personalized at scale. Previously it was manual or template-driven, which didn't convert well. We needed quality that felt editorial, low latency for live previews on the site, and predictable cost, so marketing could project spend.
[00:58] Diego: To add, we had an internal prototype using open-source models on spot instances — it worked but unpredictability in latency and infra ops overhead killed velocity.
[01:09] Jordan: Great context. Priya — can you walk us through the migration path? I know you did a small pilot first.
[01:15] Priya: Yeah. We started with the hosted API — Redwood Hosted — just to validate the prompt templates and editorial pipeline. That was quick: sign-up, keys, and we were calling it from our staging site in under a day. After two weeks of A/B tests we saw better CTRs on templates touched by LLM-based personalization. From there we moved to a Dedicated pool for predictable throughput during promotions.
[01:36] Marcus: Did you do KV cache or prefix caching at all for repeated personalization patterns?
[01:40] Priya: We leaned on Redwood's caching suggestions — the team recommended prefix cache for common product intro fragments and we implemented a small cache tier. That cut token usage by, I want to say, ~27%.
[01:52] Tom: And from a content perspective, the outputs felt more like we wanted — less robotic. We tuned the system prompts and added a short editorial pass, usually two humans for the first week, then sampled.
[02:05] Jordan: Nice. Samir, this is the part people love — specific wins. Ava, any KPIs you can share?
[02:11] Ava: Sure — we saw a 14% lift in add-to-cart from personalized descriptions vs control in Q1 after rollout. We also reduced manual writer hours by roughly 40% on product catalog work. Cost per generated SKU dropped versus our before state because Redwood's batching and dedicated pools reduced token costs during high-traffic campaigns.
[02:31] Diego: One caveat — initial latency for long multi-field prompts was higher until Marcus and Priya worked with Redwood to tune the kernel/quantization settings. But after switching model variants and enabling more aggressive batching for non-interactive backfills, latency for interactive previews dropped to sub-300ms p50.
[02:54] Marcus: I recall we ran two short benchmarks — simulated promo traffic vs normal baseline — and the Dedicated pool with continuous batching had a 2.3x cost advantage over their original self-hosted spot setup at the same latency SLO.
[03:09] Priya: That benchmark spreadsheet Marcus shared is linked in the notes — it's a small CSV; we'll attach it with the draft.
[03:16] Tom: Quick aside — the editorial team was worried about hallucinations and brand voice drift. How did you manage guardrails?
[03:23] Ava: We implemented a mix: curated prompt templates, top-k/top-p constraints, and a lightweight classification check post-generation for policy words. The human-in-the-loop for the first 2,000 SKUs helped set the templates. After that, we relied on sampling and alerts when the classifier triggered.
[03:38] Marcus: Redwood's content filters + the ability to pin model versions helped — you could roll back to a previous variant quickly.
[03:44] Diego: Security was a big ask too — SSO integration and audit logs were critical for us. Redwood's SAML SSO and request-level audit logs met our compliance checklist which sped up sign-off.
[03:58] Jordan: Were there any concerns around data residency or encryption?
[04:02] Priya: Initially yes — some PII could appear in prompts. We used Redwood's redaction guidance and opted for server-side prompt sanitization. For dedicated workloads we integrated our KMS for key management.
[04:15] Jordan: Nice. Tom, from a storytelling standpoint, anything surprising you learned after adopting LLMs?
[04:20] Tom: Two things: one, the creative teams actually loved having a fast starting point — it lowered the friction to test copy variants. Two, editorial oversight needed to move from line edits to policy sampling; it's a different workflow. Also, interestingly, customers responded better when copy referenced micro-behaviors (e.g., "people who viewed X also liked Y") which we could generate at scale.
[04:46] Ava: We tried a personalized headline experiment on homepage panels and CTR jumped 8% for segments with higher purchase intent.
[04:53] Jordan: This is golden — marketing loves numbers. Diego, any infra headaches during the Dedicated rollout?
[04:58] Diego: The main pain was IAM roles and network setup for their private deployment. We initially tested Dedicated in their VPC-connected environment; there were some firewall rules blocking telemetry endpoints. Redwood's support was responsive; we established an allowlist and confirmed endpoints. That cost us an extra day on the timeline.
[05:19] Marcus: We documented the minimal network requirements and shared a checklist which we can include in the case study appendix.
[05:25] Priya: Another small hiccup: we saw occasional tokenization differences between the local tokenizer and the hosted model which changed a few prompts slightly. Marcus helped us normalize tokens at the client side.
[05:38] Jordan: Good detail. Let's pivot a bit — for the podcast we want some soundbites. Ava, can you summarize in one line why Redwood mattered to NarrativeGrid?
[05:45] Ava: Redwood gave us reliable scale and predictable economics so we could focus on product experiments instead of firefighting infra.
[05:53] Jordan: Perfect. Diego, one-line on technical ROI?
[05:56] Diego: We cut operational hours and achieved lower per-token cost with consistent latency, which let us launch promotions without fear.
[06:03] Tom: And from the editorial side: we got higher-quality starting drafts which freed writers to focus on nuance.
[06:10] Jordan: Great. Samir — any marketing-specific asks for the case study?
[06:14] Samir: We'll need a few specific quotes (two short ones), permission to use campaign metrics, and a short on-camera testimonial if you are up for it. We can edit anything for legal sign-off.
[06:26] Ava: We're happy to do a short on-camera clip — maybe 30 seconds — and we'll sign a release.
[06:31] Diego: We'll need to run the metrics past finance for approval, but that should be fine.
[06:37] Jordan: Nice. Back to technical — Priya, can you share a high-level of the prompt templates and sampling rates you ended up using?
[06:45] Priya: Sure. Templates had three tiers: 1) headline-level (short, deterministic tokens, temperature 0.1), 2) product intro (temperature 0.2, top-p 0.9), 3) creative suggestions for A/B (temperature 0.6). For live previews we forced low temperature to ensure predictability. For creative backfills we allowed more variance.
[07:07] Marcus: We recommended disabling KV caching for the creative tier to avoid stale creative outputs.
[07:12] Tom: That makes sense. A quick human note — sometimes the low-temp outputs felt bland, so we did an editorial riff to add brand voice.
[07:21] Jordan: Switching gears — any partnerships or integrations on the roadmap with Redwood you want to call out?
[07:26] Ava: We're thinking about using Redwood Optimize recommendations as an input for our cost steering in Q3, and possibly exploring private deployment for EMEA data residency.
[07:36] Diego: Also interested in embedding generation for product recommendations and tying session signals into prompt context.
[07:44] Marcus: Redwood's embedding API and reranking could help there — we can run a pilot.
[07:49] Priya: Yes please, we have a small dataset we can share as a privacy-sanitized CSV.
[07:55] Jordan: We'll circle back on that as a separate pilot.
[07:59] Samir: For the podcast flow — do you want the Q&A to be lightly edited or raw? We usually splice for clarity and can keep it authentic.
[08:06] Ava: Light edits are fine. Keep the energy but remove uhms and long pauses.
[08:10] Tom: Also remove the small polymer of awkward silence, yeah.
[08:14] Jordan: (laughs) Noted. Okay, a couple of candid questions we sometimes get: did you ever consider continuing with your self-hosted stack instead of going to Redwood? Diego?
[08:24] Diego: We did. For pure control it's attractive, but the engineering drain — especially around kernel/hardware tuning and the ops overhead during promos — outweighed those gains. For our team size, the managed path was a better ROI.
[08:39] Ava: Also the ramp time for new features was faster with Redwood — we could try more experiments.
[08:44] Marcus: Any feature gaps you wish existed in Redwood? Priya?
[08:48] Priya: Two small things: nicer local dev tooling to emulate the Dedicated environment and a richer token-level debug view in the console. Marcus: we actually logged that feature request.
[08:59] Jordan: That's good feedback. We'll pass it to product.
[09:02] Samir: Before we close, quick lightning round — one memorable moment from the rollout?
[09:06] Ava: Launch day when personalization caused the minute-by-minute conversion rate to spike — that was pretty memorable.
[09:12] Diego: Finding a rogue firewall rule on Friday at 11pm — not my favorite.
[09:18] Tom: Seeing writers laugh at some of the early drafts — creativity wins.
[09:22] Priya: The day we saw latency fall under 300ms p50 after tuning — felt good.
[09:28] Jordan: Love it. Okay last things: Samir will draft case study and share a release form; Marcus will attach the benchmark CSV; Jordan will send the podcast audio and this raw transcript. Anything else?
[09:39] Ava: That's it from us. Thanks for having NarrativeGrid.
[09:42] Jordan: Thank you all. We'll follow up on the next steps.
